newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu keeps world guessing about plans.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu keeps world guessing about plans.

text.p: Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, his grip on his sprawling Central African nation weakening, kept the world guessing on Monday about his response to advancing rebels demanding that he stand down.

State radio said that Mobutu, who arrived back in Zaire on Friday after fresh cancer treatment, had "taken note" of a disputed vote by the transitional parliament to sack Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo.

Supporters of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, who has long coveted the job, and even supporters of Mobutu and Kengo aides, said the veteran president's comments suggested that Kengo was finished.
Mobutu, making his first public outing since his return home, told journalists on Sunday he came back to take care of Zaire's higher interests -- in particular its unity and territorial integrity.
Asked about his plans and whether he would negotiate with Kabila, he replied: "In the next 48 hours you will know."

A senior South African official, who was on a delegation that had talks with Mobutu on Sunday, said in Cape Town on Monday that Mobutu was due to make a major announcement -- possibly before the end of the day.

"Possibly even by this evening, he will have made those announcements which we hope will be leading us to finding a solution to that problem there," Anthony Mongalo, deputy director-general of the department of foreign affairs, said.
The Organisation of African Unity holds a special summit on the five-month-old civil war on Wednesday. Host Togo says both Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila have been invited.
Togo's foreign minister, Pierre Koffi Panou, told Reuters that Kabila had agreed to send a delegation. "That's a positive step," he said by telephone from Lome.
Diplomatic efforts to end the war have focused on calls for a truce and talks.
The U.N. Security Council came up with a ceasefire plan, which the Zairean government accept.
Mobutu called for a truce and talks before leaving France for home but Kabila says talks must come first.
U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun had talks with Kabila in Zaire's captured second city of Kisangani on Saturday but Kabila stood firm -- with 10,000 enthusiastic supporters calling for the war to continue.

The South African team, led by Nelson Mandela's deputy Thabo Mbeki, delivered a letter from Mandela outlining proposals for solving the crisis at the heart of Central Africa, already a volatile region.

The rebels, who control, one fifth of Zaire, say their forces are 200 km (125 miles) from the southern mining capital of Lubumbashi and half that distance from the diamond-mining capital of Mbuji-Mayi.
The United States, France and Belgium, the former colonial power, have sent troops to the region, ready to rescue their citizens should that prove necessary.
